opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real tension, and I don't think there's a single right answer. On one hand, you have to be honest about what the data tells us. If you look at what happened in language and vision, a lot of the breakthroughs came from scale: scale of data, scale of compute, scale of engineering. Robotics is probably not going to be an exception. Collecting large amounts of diverse, high-quality robot interaction data is extremely expensive. You need fleets of hardware, teleoperators, infrastructure to maintain it all. That's something a single academic lab, or even a consortium of labs, can't easily do. So I understand why companies with a lot of capital are going after it, and frankly I think it's good for the field. They're stress-testing the hypothesis that scale alone gets you to general-purpose robots.

On the other hand, I'm a little cautious about the idea that this is the *only* path, or that we should all just wait for one or two big players to collect the data and train the giant model. Robotics is different from language in some important ways. There isn't an internet of robot data lying around. The embodiment matters: different robots, different sensors, different tasks. And the physical world has a very long tail. So I think there are a lot of open scientific questions that aren't purely about throwing more money at the problem. How do you learn efficiently from a small amount of data? How do you use human videos, simulation, or other cheaper sources of supervision? How do you get robots to improve themselves once they're deployed? How do you structure models so they generalize compositionally rather than memorizing? Those are questions where academia can contribute a lot, sometimes more effectively, because we can take risks on ideas that don't have an immediate commercial payoff.

So the way I see it, it's more of an ecosystem. The centralized, capital-heavy efforts are pushing on the scaling frontier, and they'll tell us a lot about what scale can and can't buy. Meanwhile, the more distributed research community should focus on the things that make scaling cheaper, smarter, or unnecessary in certain regimes. And ideally there's a healthy exchange between the two: open datasets, shared benchmarks, open models. I'd be worried if the field became too closed and everything happened behind company walls, because robotics really benefits from many people trying many different things. But I'm optimistic. We're seeing more open-source models and cross-institution data efforts, and I think that kind of collaboration is going to matter a lot for getting robots into the real world.

r001.rationale: The response supports capital-heavy efforts as useful for testing how far scale can take robotics, while acknowledging that scale alone may not deliver general-purpose robots and that it may not be the only path.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because I sit in kind of an awkward spot. I'm a professor at Georgia Tech, I run a lab with graduate students, and I also spend time in industry at NVIDIA. So I see both sides of this pretty directly.

I think the honest answer is that there's a real tension, and I don't want to pretend it away. If you look at what happened in language models, the frontier work moved almost entirely into a handful of companies, because the recipe became "collect an enormous amount of data, buy an enormous amount of compute, and scale." And a lot of people are now betting that robotics will follow the same path: you build fleets of robots, you collect millions of hours of teleoperation data, you train a giant foundation model, and that's going to require billions of dollars and a very centralized operation. If that's the whole story, then academia is basically a spectator.

But I actually don't think robotics is at that stage yet, and I'd push back on the assumption that it's purely a scaling problem. With language, the data already existed. The internet was there. For robots, we don't have that. Nobody has figured out what the "internet of robot data" even looks like, what the right representation is, how much of it can come from simulation or from human video versus real robot interaction. Those are fundamentally open research questions, and they're not questions that money alone answers. You can burn a lot of capital collecting the wrong data.

So the way I think about my role, and I think the role of academia more broadly, is that we should be doing the things that a centralized, capital-driven effort is structurally bad at. Big organizations have to commit to a bet. Once you've bought ten thousand robots and hired a few hundred teleoperators, you are locked into that paradigm, and it becomes very hard to question it. Academia can afford to be the place where people ask, "Wait, is this even the right approach?" We can try the weird ideas, the ones where the expected payoff is low but the upside is that you change what everyone else is doing. Things like better ways to learn from human video, structured representations for long-horizon tasks, learning from much smaller amounts of data. Those are the kinds of questions my students work on.

The other thing I'd say is that the ecosystem actually needs a counterweight. If the only people who can do robot learning research are inside three companies, then the field loses a lot of diversity of thought, and honestly a lot of talent, because the pipeline of people who learned to do this work comes from universities. So part of what I care about is building open tools, open benchmarks, simulation environments, things that let a student with one robot arm and a few GPUs still contribute something meaningful. That's not a nice-to-have, I think it's necessary for the field to stay healthy.

And then practically, I just don't think it's an either-or. I collaborate with industry, my students intern at these companies, some of them go work there. The scale efforts and the small-scale research actually feed each other. The big labs need ideas and people, and the academic labs benefit from seeing what breaks at scale. So I'm not anti-centralization. I think some of that is inevitable and probably good for getting robots into the world. I just don't want the entire field to collapse into one strategy before we actually know it's the right one.

r001.rationale: The response says some centralized scaling is inevitable and probably useful, but it does not judge that large-scale robotics development should be attempted despite the possibility of falling short of expectations.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real tension there. Large-scale robotics takes a lot of resources—hardware, infrastructure, people, and time—so there are practical reasons for bringing that effort together. You can coordinate development and tackle problems that would be very difficult for a small team to solve alone.

But I wouldn’t equate concentrating resources with concentrating all the ideas. If only a few organizations can participate, then their priorities can end up defining what the whole field works on. And we still have so much to learn in robotics that we need room for different approaches.

So, to me, the question is how to make that investment create opportunities beyond the organization making it. Can we share tools, make platforms more accessible, and let smaller groups test ideas without rebuilding the entire infrastructure? I see a role for large, capital-intensive efforts, but I’d want them to support a broader research ecosystem.

r001.rationale: The response supports a role for large, capital-intensive robotics efforts, but does not say they are necessary to attempt despite the possibility of falling short of expectations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real tension there. Large-scale robotics requires resources: hardware, infrastructure, people who can maintain the robots, and a lot of experimentation. Having a centralized effort can make that easier because you can coordinate all those pieces and work toward a common goal.

But I don’t think that means all the important ideas have to come from those organizations. The concern is what happens when access to that infrastructure becomes a prerequisite for contributing. Then you risk narrowing the kinds of questions people can ask and the kinds of applications they pursue.

So I would want those efforts to create opportunities for broader participation—through shared tools, access to platforms, and research that other people can build on. Capital can help us get systems working at scale, but we should also ask whether that progress makes it easier for the next person to contribute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the resources and tradeoffs involved in large-scale robotics, but does not say that attempting it is necessary despite the possibility of falling short of expectations.
